statements.anchor: Ask AI for more readable or efficient implementations.
statements.label: AI for alternative implementations
statements.passage:
Effective use of AI has become a core skill in modern computer science and related fields. I encourage you to use AI in this course to build your proficiency. However, with freedom comes responsibility: use AI to enhance your learning, not replace it. You must find balance in your usage so that you learn effectively — this looks different for everyone and requires experimentation.

A primary goal of this course is to prepare you as an AI tool builder. That requires hands-on practice with coding, design, and analysis. If AI does that heavy lifting for you, you have gone too far. Here are a few ideas to guide your AI usage:

Code review:
Write a method yourself, then have AI help you check your work. Make sure you understand any suggestions or fixes the AI proposes. Never accept fixes blindly; your solution may be better aligned with the project goals.

Explore alternative implementations:
Ask AI for more readable or efficient implementations. You might learn about an approach that you did not consider!

Mock quizzes:
Have AI quiz you on concepts, code, or results.

Ultimately, you are responsible for all the code and analyses that you turn in; AI cannot take the blame for shortcomings.
Here are several points to keep in mind:

For base projects, you should only use Python packages listed in
Software
. Do not let AI convince you otherwise.

Be cautious of AI suggestions that involve esoteric or exotic functions or overly complex implementations. If you cannot read and understand them, do not include them!

statements.anchor: you can use generative AI systems to learn about concepts iteratively through a conversation
statements.label: AI for concepts via conversation
statements.passage:
Generative AI systems (like Claude, ChatGPT, etc), if used correctly, can serve as powerful tools for learning and idea refinement. In this course, you can use generative AI systems to learn about concepts iteratively through a conversation (much like you would have a conversation with a peer, TA or an instructor). However, you cannot ask these systems to directly give you answers or write code for you. This is because I believe the intellectual growth you can get from working through a difficult problem and discovering the answer for yourself cannot be replicated by just reading a pre-generated answer — and the skills you learn from this course, such as applying algorithmic reasoning to justify correctness, is more important than ever as AI increasingly lowers the barrier to generating code.

Here are some concrete rules that exemplify this (but are not intended to be comprehensive):

Do NOT:
* Give the model a problem description and ask it to sketch an algorithm for you or write you pseudo code.
* Give the model the homework description and ask it to organize the code for you (e.g., generate the necessary function headers, write the main functions etc).
* Give the model a function description and ask it to generate code for you.
* Given some problem description or code, ask the model to generate test cases for you.
* Use the model to write any aspect of the justification of correctness document.

Using the AI system in ways as described above will count as cheating even if you cite the AI system as a source.

You CAN:
* Ask clarification questions about the fundamentals of programming (e.g., “When should I use a public vs. private method in Java?”)
* Ask for conceptual clarifications (e.g., “What is the difference between average case and best case run times?”)
* Try to work through the logic of something you don’t understand (e.g., “Why is the run time of this algorithm [describe] n^2?”)
* Given a problem description and your proposed algorithm and “talk” through the potential fallacies.

Note, for any of these models having the correct “prompt” is necessary. So you may have varying levels of success using these models to gain conceptual understanding, and in many cases just talking to your instructors/ TA/ peers or even doing straight up googling is likely to yield better results. If you do decide to use these models, it is your responsibility to also fact check the insights that you gain.

AI policy.

You may be learning something incorrectly if you rely on these tools. If you use them, it is best to double-check information with a more reliable source, such as a textbook.

Example: Suppose the homework assignment is: “Prove that binary search makes at most log(n) comparisons.” A student may use an external textbook, website, or AI tool to learn more about how binary search works. Usage of Gen AI tools
​

Developing strong competencies in the skills associated with this course, from student-based brainstorming to project development, will prepare you for success in your degree pathway and, ultimately, a competitive career. Therefore, the use of generative AI tools to complete any aspect of assignments for this course are discouraged.

However, in principle you may submit AI-generated code, or code that is based on or derived from AI-generated code, as long as this use is properly documented in the comments: you need to include the prompt and the significant parts of the response. AI tools may help you avoid syntax errors, but there is no guarantee that the generated code is correct. It is your responsibility to identify errors in program logic through comprehensive, documented testing. Moreover, generated code, even if syntactically correct, may have significant scope for improvement, in particular regarding separation of concerns and avoiding repetitions. The submission itself should meet our standards of attribution and validation.

Significant deviations from the provided requirements on assignments, or lack of citations of Gen AI usage as stated, in your submission, will be treated as violation of this policy. It will also be counted as plagiarism and will result in a 0. Multiple violations will lead to a report to the Honor Code council and more severe Academic sanctions.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude are increasingly powerful and might be capable of solving some of the assignments.
However, the assignments must be your own work and the use of these tools for generating assignment solutions is prohibited (will be treated as a violation of academic integrity)
.
Assignment will be penalized with a negative grade if you used Gen AI, and you will fail the course if you use Gen AI in any exam (Unit and/or Final) or you repeat a misconduct in an assignment.

There are multiple reasons why these tools are detrimental to your learning experience:

They rob you of the ability to think and learn the concepts for yourself since solving problems is an essential step to gaining a solid understanding of the material.

You will struggle with the in-classroom quizzes and exams where you will not have access to these tools.

While we acknowledge that these tools are likely to become an important of a software engineer’s workflow in the future, you are much more likely to use these tools in an effective manner if you already have expertise in the relevant technical topics. Developing such expertise requires putting in the effort to learn these topics without the assistance of these tools.

These tools are prone to generating imperfect or even incorrect solutions, so trusting them blindly can lead to bad consequences.

Ultimately, you will get out of the class what you put in. Simply copying and pasting code from ChatGPT/Claude will not lead to any learning. If you are stuck on the assignments, reach out to the course staff. The course staff is here to help you!

We allow the use of AI in this course, but warn that you may miss valuable insights from doing the work yourself, which can leave you less prepared for industry. Treat tools that provide AI assistance (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Llama, etc.) as if they were a person outside of class who knows nothing about the project.

Students find it more useful for some aspects of the course than others. AI can be a useful tool to explain things you don’t understand. Asking AI to write text, code, or tests for this course project can be problematic and hurt the team’s score and yours. Teams have lost more project points than they gained and removed the AI-generated code to improve their grades. AI produces simplistic test cases compared to those used for grading.

If you copy substantial amounts of text into and out of a chat interface, you are likely compromising your education.

statements.anchor: You may not submit work the work of others and claim it as your own.
statements.label: no claiming others' work as own
statements.passage:
The academic integrity policy is for CS 1110 is defined by a single principle.

You may not submit work the work of others and claim it as your own.

This can be the work of other people in the class. This can be the work of
generative AI (e.g. code generated that you did write other than via a
natural language prompt). If you did not do the work yourself, you must be
honest about it, or it is an academic integrity violation. To not disclose this
fact is a form of academic
fraud
.

Note that both sides of the “and” are required for it to be violation. If you
submit work, but are honest who or what was involved in creating it, it is not
an academic integrity violation. Some work of the work that you will do in this
course is expected to be done with other people, so when you submit it your are
not claiming as solely your own.

When we prosecute cases of academic integrity, our primary concern is for the
student that submitted work without properly attributing its source. However,
there is the issue of students that
enable
academic integrity violations.
What happens if you give your assignment to another student and they then pass
that work off as their own?

In that case, we will only prosecute for an academic integrity violation if you
were reasonably aware of that the other student would pass if off as their own
work. In that case you are part of a
conspiracy to commit fraud
. This may
sound sinister, but
conspiracy
is just a legal term meaning a plan by two
or more people to do something not permitted. We have more on this in the
section on
preventing violations
below.

Note that the side effect of this principle is that you are allowed to use
generative AI for code that you do not submit to us. So you can use it to
create practice problems for yourself. But we strongly recommend that you
limit such work to a chat interface and refrain from agentic tools such as
Codex or Claude, as those can hurt your skill training.

ChatGPT 5.6 was used for brainstorming. Some ideas in the solution came from GPT, some from me and my homework partners. All of the words in this solution were written by me.

Gemini 3.2 wrote the entire solution. I checked Gemini's response for correctness and copied it here.

Special note on Artificial Intelligence-based code generators

AI-based tools such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Code Llama, and others can generate code for you based on natural language prompts that you provide. For this class, I do
not
consider it to be an honor principle violation for
you
to use these tools to create or debug
your
short assignment or problem set solutions. However, I strongly urge you to write the solutions yourself, rather than relying on these tools. Most of the true mastery of this course's material happens from striving to create correct and efficient code yourself, not from simply reading and copying an AI-based tool's code. Additionally, these tools will not be available on the midterms and final, so you'll need to fully understand the course material to succeed.

If you choose to use an AI-based tool you
must
:

Cite the tool you used for each method (function) created or debugged with one of these tools, even if you modify the tool-produced code

Be able to explain every line of code in your solution; specifically what the line does and why you included it.

If you choose to use an AI-based tool you
must not
:

Share the prompts you used with anyone (other than your partner, where partners are permitted)

Share the tool's output with anyone (other than your partner, where partners are permitted). Other students must use the tool themselves and must evaluate the tool's output relative to their solution

Use Java-provided classes or methods that we have not discussed in class. For example, if an AI-based tool suggests you use a class such as a Set, but we haven't covered Sets yet, you may not use them until we cover them. Once we've covered a concept in class, you may use Java-provided code unless specifically instructed not to use it.

Remember: because code compiles and runs does not mean it is correct or efficient. Also, be aware that these tools typically store and analyze your prompts, potentially building a profile of you.

assignments, lab exercises, and exam questions in this course. The

instructions by the instructor to use a generative AI tool in the

generative AI may in general inhibit development, practice, or
understanding of those skills.

own will violate DePaul’s Academic Integrity Policy and could result
in failure of the assignment or the course.

statements.label: AI helpful for learning
statements.passage:
You, your peers, the Internet, and AI-assisted tools like ChatGPT will be helpful in learning the material in Compsci 201.
All your work, even when done collaboratively, is your responsibility in terms of being able to demonstrate understanding, knowledge,
and mastery of the material. Each student taking 201 has their own goals for what they expect, why they are taking the course,
and how they will continue to study computer science. If you cannot complete the work of the course without extensive reliance
on the Internet, peers, and AI-assistance, you will likely not succeed in further studies, in finding an internship/job, or perhaps
in feeling good about what you've done.

For in-class exams and for APT quizzes, **you may not use any AI-assistance. No computers or electronic devices may be used in completing exams.
** For these assessments, we expect strict adherence to the Duke Community Standard and we will use similarity-detection and other tools
as part of ensuring that is the case.

**If you are found to have violated these terms for any exam (midterm and final) you will earn 0% credit for that exam
as well as an additional letter-grade deduction of your final grade.** If you are found to have violated these terms for any part of
an APT quiz you will earn 0% credit for all APT quizzes during the semester, even if you've previously earned credit.

For APTs (not quizzes), projects, and discussion we explicitly encourage collaboration, though
that should not mean showing your code to someone except for help with debugging unless you're working on a
project that allows a partner --- in which case you should only be working with your partner.

### Academic honesty

For programming projects, course staff will review your work simply to see how you make progress.
We do not run software similarity detection tools on code submitted for projects. We do ask you to list all
students and staff you've talked with in completing each project.

For APT quizzes, you're required to work alone and without using ChatGPT or other LLMs or CoPilot.
The recording of your screen is one way we see your work. We also review every APT submission as part of ascertaining
that your work is your own. We do run software similarity detection tools comparing your work with solutions turned in by
other students as well as solutions developed by ChatGPT and other LLMs. Please see the section above about violations of the
Duke Community Standard and course rules with respect to APT quizz
